patient.chief_complaint: Worsening mood, paranoia, and 'manic episode' for 9 days according to treating psychiatrist
patient.history_present_illness: A 25-year-old left-handed woman with a 2-year history of bipolar disorder type II, well-controlled on lamotrigine and quetiapine, was brought to the ED by her psychiatrist after failing to respond to adjustments in her psychiatric medications over the past 9 days. Her psychiatrist describes her as having been in remission for 14 months prior to this presentation. The behavioral change began approximately 10-11 days ago with worsening insomnia, grandiosity, and pressured speech, initially attributed by her psychiatrist to a hypomanic episode. Over the following days, however, the psychiatric symptoms became more severe and atypical for her prior episodes, including features of paranoia (believing she was being surveilled by her neighbors), visual illusions (seeing 'shadows moving'), and on two occasions echolalic speech that was noted by her mother. She also developed a new repetitive behavior of pulling at her hair and rubbing her face in a stereotyped fashion, which her psychiatrist recognized as abnormal for a bipolar episode. Her psychiatrist increased quetiapine to 200 mg and added risperidone 1 mg without improvement. She has had no witnessed generalized seizures. She did not have a recent febrile illness but did report a period of severe fatigue and mild sore throat about five weeks ago. Her weight has dropped 4 kg over the past 10 days due to refusal to eat. Lamotrigine level was checked two days ago and was within therapeutic range. The psychiatrist is concerned this is not a typical bipolar episode and has referred her to the ED for further evaluation.

differential.key_features: Known bipolar diagnosis, prior hypomanic episodes — but absence of response to mood stabilizers, new chorea, echolalia, and autonomic instability are atypical for bipolar disorder
On antipsychotics (risperidone added), mildly elevated CK, autonomic instability — but CK only 198 (not >1000), no lead-pipe rigidity, no extreme hyperthermia; autoimmune encephalitis is more likely
THC positive on UDS — but last use 1 month ago, residual metabolites only, cannabis does not explain chorea or autonomic instability
Family history of SLE, weakly positive ANA — but anti-dsDNA negative, complement normal, no systemic lupus features

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduce NMS risk and encephalitis exacerbation

critical_actions: Recognize that prior psychiatric diagnosis does not preclude new organic brain disease
Discontinue recently added risperidone — antipsychotics worsen anti-NMDAR encephalitis outcomes
Perform continuous EEG — extreme delta brush pattern is pathognomonic
Anti-NMDAR antibody testing is mandatory when bipolar patient fails to respond to escalated psychiatric medications with new atypical features (chorea, echolalia, dyskinesias)
contraindicated_actions: Attributing all symptoms to bipolar exacerbation and escalating antipsychotics without organic workup
High-dose antipsychotics (haloperidol, high-dose risperidone) in anti-NMDAR encephalitis
Diagnosing cannabis-induced psychosis based on positive drug screen without further workup
Attributing choreiform movements to tardive dyskinesia from prior antipsychotic use
key_reasoning_points: A known psychiatric diagnosis (bipolar disorder) should never preclude workup for a new organic neurological disorder when the presentation changes character
Choreiform movements, echolalia, and orofacial dyskinesias in a 'bipolar' patient are classic clues for anti-NMDAR encephalitis
Autonomic instability (tachycardia, diaphoresis, blood pressure lability) is a feature of anti-NMDAR encephalitis that distinguishes it from primary psychiatric disorders
Extreme delta brush on continuous EEG is pathognomonic for anti-NMDAR encephalitis — routine 30-minute EEG may miss this finding
Antipsychotics prescribed empirically worsen outcomes in anti-NMDAR encephalitis and carry NMS risk in this encephalitis setting
Large teratoma (4.1 cm) found — teratoma resection is a critical therapeutic intervention, not just diagnostic
